text: By now a control has been written as code, tested in audit or report-only mode, piloted, and rolled out in waves without a business revolt. That's a real engineering achievement, and it still hasn't answered the question that actually matters: did the organization get measurably safer because of it? A control can be live, enforced, and perfectly stable while quietly doing nothing to reduce the risk it was built for. Shipping and working are two different claims, and only measurement tells you if the second one is true.

You can't tell if anything changed if you never recorded what "before" looked like. Before a new MFA-enforcing policy ships, pull the real numbers: how many account-compromise alerts fired last month, how many legacy-authentication sign-ins were logged, what the relevant Secure Score control's point value already is. Write those numbers down with a date, the same way the control itself gets committed to a repository — a baseline that exists only in someone's memory isn't a baseline at all.

After rollout, measure the exact same metrics, over the same window length, against that same baseline. An 81 percent drop in risky sign-in alerts and a near-elimination of legacy authentication traffic is real evidence the policy did what it was built to do. A single good-looking week right after rollout, with no defined baseline to compare it against, isn't evidence at all — it's an anecdote dressed up as a result.

Microsoft Secure Score assigns point values to specific configured controls and rolls them into one compliance percentage, so a properly enforced MFA policy moves the score up. That's useful corroboration — it confirms the control is actually configured the way you think — but it measures configuration, not outcomes. The incident and alert counts are what tell you risk actually went down; Secure Score is the second signal confirming the configuration behind that drop is intact.

Writing a control as code, testing it safely, rolling it out without breaking the business, and proving it actually reduced risk — that's the full engineering loop this chapter built. Chapter 8's capstone puts all four habits to work in one lab: designing an identity architecture for a company merger.
